The dynamics of soccer games can be complex, making it challenging to predict their outcome even for sports enthusiasts. In a 11 vs 11 game, numerous factors like ball possession, shots on goal, and scoring, intertwine in multifaceted ways, hindering straightforward prediction. Furthermore, the three-dimensional nature of the game on the field, combined with uncertainty over players' intentions and physical states, adds to the difficulty. In a 1-on-1 situation, the outcome often depends on various factors including the players' speed, direction of approach, ball control ability, and prior actions. Despite the complexity, the outcome of such situations can be classified into a limited number of categories, making it possible to use a policy learning approach to determine the most effective action for a player in a similar situation. In this study, we employed a deep deterministic policy gradient algorithm to learn an optimal playing strategy in critical 1-on-1 situations on the soccer field. Although the algorithm generates realistic playing scenarios, it may suffer from biases towards actions that increase the player's control over the ball, potentially leading to biased outcomes. To rectify this, we employed the "importance sampling" technique to adjust the policy so that it mirrors the true distribution of situations on the soccer field. As a result, the player's physical position and direction of movement no longer had an impact on the situation's outcome when analyzed. Moreover, our playing strategy was found to be more effective than standard playing styles, both in isolated situations and in simulated soccer games. In conclusion, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of policy learning in soccer playing tactics, highlights the importance of correcting biased outcomes, and provides a framework for using data from sports platforms to train playing policies. It also serves as a reference model for similar studies in other sports. Finally, the underlying methods are available on GitHub for use in analyzing other sports data. The code is available at https://github.com/ghsyhw/PolicyLearningSoccer. The present study introduces a cost-effective method for obtaining two-dimensional velocity vector measurements using a single-point Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV) system. This technique, called the Distant Operation of a Single-Point LDV System to Acquire 2D Measurements, enables the calculation of velocity vectors at multiple points in a flow field through careful positioning of seeding particles and measurement locations. This technique's effectiveness was validated in a low-speed air flow over a flat plate with a circular hole, where the results showed excellent agreement with prespecified values when the hole was located near the center of the flat plate. When the hole was moved further away from the center, some discrepancies arose due to insufficent particle density on the far side of the plate, leading to inaccurate vector calculations. This issue was resolved by employing a particle generator on the far side of the plate, resulting in highly accurate two-dimensional velocity vector maps even when the hole was positioned at a greater distance. This improved setup was applied to a more complex flow over a NACA0015 airfoil, yielding detailed velocity vector distributions throughout the flow field. This research provides a practical guide for implementing this technique, highlighting the importance of careful particle seeding and optimizing the LDV system's viewing angle to ensure successful two-dimensional velocity vector measurements. This technique's effectiveness was further demonstrated by comparing its results to a 25m^2 2D Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) system in the flat plate experiment, showing the distant operation method yields similar accuracy to the PIV system when the hole is located near the center of the flat plate. Using 3D numerical models that simulate the internal dynamics of the three planets, we investigated various scenarios to determine the possible causes of Venus' unique rotation characteristics. After examining different angular momentum transfer models, both theoretical and observed, we found that an massive impact that dug a crater over a billion kilometers deep would be necessary to slow down Earth's rotation, contradicting geological evidence. Furthermore, we discovered that such an event would also disrupt Mars' obliquity, making it difficult to explain the low axis tilt of less than 25 degrees.
